opts: Correct. The risk of progression from monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance to myeloma is about 1% per year. Her low M-protein, under 10% plasma cells and lack of myeloma-defining features keep her in this low-risk precursor stage.
About 10% per year is the progression rate of smoldering myeloma, the intermediate stage with an M-protein above 3 g/dL and 10-60% plasma cells. Tell: her precursor is lower risk, about 1% per year.
A quarter per year greatly overstates the risk for this asymptomatic precursor. Tell: the figure for her is about 1% per year.
A risk above 50% (within 2 years) applies to some high-risk smoldering myeloma groups, not to her. Tell: low M-protein and few plasma cells mean about 1% per year.

His beta-2 microglobulin is 6.4 mg/L (normal 0.8-2.2 mg/L) and albumin 3.8 g/dL (normal 3.5-5.0 g/dL); chromosomal studies show only standard-risk abnormalities, and lactate dehydrogenase is normal. What is his R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) stage?
opts: His albumin, chromosomes and lactate dehydrogenase fit stage I, but stage I also needs beta-2 microglobulin below 3.5 mg/L, and his is 6.4. Tell: one failed stage I item drops him out of stage I.

Correct. Stage III needs all of beta-2 microglobulin at least 5.5 mg/L, high-risk chromosomes and high lactate dehydrogenase; he has only the high beta-2 microglobulin. Stage I needs beta-2 microglobulin below 3.5 mg/L, and his is 6.4. Not stage I or III is stage II.

A beta-2 microglobulin above 5.5 mg/L alone is not enough; stage III also requires high-risk chromosomes and high lactate dehydrogenase, and both of his are favorable. Tell: the stage III criteria are joined by 'and'.
There is no R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) stage IV; the table has stages I to III. Tell: a mixed picture is stage II.

opts: Allogeneic stem cell transplant is not first treatment for new, asymptomatic indolent follicular lymphoma. Tell: indolent, asymptomatic disease is observed.

Rapid transfer of care fits Burkitt lymphoma, and hospitalization fits aggressive lymphoma with electrolyte abnormalities; her disease has waxed and waned for 2 years. Tell: an indolent course needs no admission.

Correct. Follicular lymphoma, the most common indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma, frequently needs no treatment (watch and wait); intermittent low-intensity therapy is used if symptomatic. She is asymptomatic, so observation fits.

Multi-drug chemotherapy is for aggressive B-cell lymphoma or high-risk follicular disease; she has indolent, asymptomatic disease. Tell: waxing and waning painless nodes with no symptoms are observed.

opts: Under 10% treats a very aggressive lymphoma as hopeless; early, prompt multi-agent chemotherapy gives children above 90% long-term survival. Tell: fast-growing does not mean incurable here.
About 25% understates the outcome; treated early, children with Burkitt lymphoma do very well, above 90%. Tell: the prognosis is excellent with prompt therapy.
50-90% is the range quoted for adults; children do better, above 90%. Tell: the pediatric figure is the higher one.

Correct. With early identification and multi-agent chemotherapy, Burkitt lymphoma has an excellent long-term prognosis: above 90% in children and 50-90% in adults. Prompt treatment, with care for tumor lysis, is what earns that outcome.

set1.q: A 27-year-old man has a persistent, enlarging 3-cm painless supraclavicular lymph node. Excisional biopsy shows a few large Reed-Sternberg cells (binucleated, neoplastic B cells) among numerous immune cells. Which marker pattern confirms classical Hodgkin lymphoma?
opts: A cyclin D1 translocation is not a Hodgkin marker; his biopsy shows Reed-Sternberg cells, which classical Hodgkin lymphoma pairs with CD15 (cluster of differentiation 15) and CD30 (cluster of differentiation 30). Tell: a young man with Reed-Sternberg cells has Hodgkin lymphoma.
Translocation t(14;18) placing the BCL-2 (B-cell lymphoma 2) gene

A t(14;18) translocation is not a Hodgkin marker; classical Hodgkin lymphoma is confirmed by CD15 (cluster of differentiation 15) and CD30 (cluster of differentiation 30) on the excisional biopsy. Tell: binucleated Reed-Sternberg cells mean classical Hodgkin markers.
CD15 (cluster of differentiation 15) and CD30 (cluster of differentiation 30)

Correct. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma expresses CD15 (cluster of differentiation 15) and CD30 (cluster of differentiation 30). Its few malignant Reed-Sternberg cells (binucleated, neoplastic B cells) sit among numerous immune effector cells, which his biopsy shows.
CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) and CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5)

CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) and CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5) are not the Reed-Sternberg pattern; classical Hodgkin lymphoma expresses CD15 (cluster of differentiation 15) and CD30 (cluster of differentiation 30). Tell: Reed-Sternberg cells in a node point to the CD15 (cluster of differentiation 15) and CD30 (cluster of differentiation 30) pattern.

set1.q: A 61-year-old woman has smoldering multiple myeloma: M-protein 3.6 g/dL and 18% clonal bone marrow plasma cells, with no anemia, bone lesions, renal failure or hypercalcemia. No high-risk subgroup feature is identified. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Correct. Smoldering myeloma typically does not require treatment, although early intervention may be considered for some high-risk subgroups; she has none identified. It progresses at about 10% per year, so monitoring continues.
A proteasome inhibitor, immunomodulatory drug and steroid regimen treats myeloma, which is symptomatic by definition; she has no myeloma-defining event. Tell: smoldering disease is typically watched.
Autologous transplant improves survival in active myeloma after initial therapy, not in smoldering disease. Tell: no CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) feature, no transplant.
Allopurinol and fluids prevent tumor lysis before treating aggressive lymphoma. Tell: smoldering myeloma is monitored, with no tumor lysis concern.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man has an absolute lymphocyte count of 25,000 per microliter (normal 1,000-4,000) for 4 months and no symptoms. Flow cytometry is sent on his peripheral blood. Which result supports chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Binucleated Reed-Sternberg cells expressing CD15 (cluster of differentiation 15) and CD30 (cluster of differentiation 30) are classical Hodgkin lymphoma, found on node biopsy, not in blood lymphocytosis. Tell: CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) with CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5) is the leukemia's pattern.
A reactive, non-clonal lymphocytosis fits infection (such as pertussis), not leukemia, which arises from a clone of mature B cells. Tell: chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a clonal B-cell disease.

Clonal plasma cells making a single antibody, most commonly IgG, are multiple myeloma, a marrow disease with CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) features. Tell: circulating clonal B lymphocytes are chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Correct. Flow cytometry confirms chronic lymphocytic leukemia by identifying a clonal B-cell population with coexpression of CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) and CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5) on the lymphocytes. With his count above 5,000 for 3 months, that confirms it.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman has nodal marginal zone lymphoma, a low-grade B-cell lymphoma, involving several node regions above the diaphragm. She has developed bothersome symptoms and now needs treatment, but her disease is not extensive. Which agent is used?
opts: Allopurinol prevents tumor lysis in aggressive lymphoma; it does not treat the lymphoma. Tell: a symptomatic low-grade B-cell lymphoma gets the anti-CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20) antibody.

Correct. Low-grade B-cell lymphomas are treated with rituximab (an anti-CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20) monoclonal antibody) when treatment is required, with chemotherapy added if the disease is extensive. Hers needs treatment but is not extensive.

That multi-drug chemotherapy without rituximab is the T-cell lymphoma regimen; hers is a B-cell lymphoma that expresses CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20). Tell: a low-grade B-cell lymphoma needing treatment gets rituximab.
That four-drug combination is the Hodgkin lymphoma chemotherapy regimen. Tell: her disease is a low-grade non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma, treated with rituximab.

set1.q: A 52-year-old woman has diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes, the liver and the bone marrow. Her ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) performance status is 1, and her lactate dehydrogenase is normal. How many poor-prognosis factors does she have?
opts: One counts the organ disease once but misses that it scores twice: extranodal sites and stage IV are separate items on the list. Tell: liver and marrow involvement give both.

Correct. Item by item: age over 60, no (52); extranodal sites, yes (liver and marrow); ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) status above 2, no (1); stage III or IV, yes (multiple organs is stage 4); elevated lactate dehydrogenase, no. Total 2.
Three adds an item she lacks: she is 52, not over 60, and her lactate dehydrogenase is normal. Tell: only extranodal sites and stage IV count.
Four would need two more of: age over 60, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, or a performance status above 2; she has none of these. Tell: she scores on extranodal disease and stage only.

set1.q: A 46-year-old man was treated with chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 25 and has been in remission since. He now has new cytopenias, and marrow evaluation shows a myelodysplastic syndrome. How is this best explained?
opts: Richter transformation is chronic lymphocytic leukemia turning into an aggressive B-cell lymphoma. Tell: he never had that leukemia; his risk comes from prior Hodgkin therapy.
The 10-fold sibling risk concerns developing Hodgkin lymphoma itself, not later myelodysplasia. Tell: myelodysplasia after old chemotherapy is a delayed toxicity.
A delayed toxicity of his therapy

Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma is generally curable (more than 90% alive at 5 years), but survivors may have delayed toxicities, including myelodysplastic syndrome, secondary leukemia and other cancers. Two decades after chemotherapy, his new marrow disease fits.
Relapse would return as lymphoma (nodes, mediastinal mass), not as a myelodysplastic marrow. Tell: a new marrow cancer years later is a delayed treatment toxicity.

set1.q: A 71-year-old farmer with newly diagnosed chronic lymphocytic leukemia asks whether the pesticides he sprayed for decades caused his leukemia. Which response is accurate?
opts: Radiation is an environmental risk factor listed for multiple myeloma, not for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: there is no known occupational or environmental risk for this leukemia.
No exposure is a known risk

Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia has no known occupational or environmental risk factors. Its risk factors are age (median onset 70), male sex (twice as common), and Eastern European or Jewish descent.

Farming and pesticides are listed as environmental risk factors for lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia), not for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: this leukemia has no known occupational risk factors.
Hepatitis C is associated with splenic marginal zone lymphoma, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: his leukemia's risks are age, male sex and ancestry, not infection or exposure.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man has monoclonal B lymphocytosis: an absolute lymphocyte count of 4,300 per microliter (normal 1,000-4,000) with a clonal B-cell population and no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms. He asks how often this progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Which rate is accurate?
opts: Correct. Monoclonal B lymphocytosis progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia at a rate of about 1-2% per year. His count below 5,000 with no nodes, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms keeps him in the precursor state for now.
About 10% per year is the progression rate of smoldering myeloma to multiple myeloma, not of monoclonal B lymphocytosis. Tell: the B-cell precursor progresses at 1-2% per year.
A quarter per year greatly overstates the risk; monoclonal B lymphocytosis progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia at about 1-2% per year. Tell: it is a slow, low-rate precursor.
A risk above 50% within 2 years is quoted for some high-risk smoldering myeloma groups, not for monoclonal B lymphocytosis. Tell: this precursor progresses at about 1-2% per year.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man has cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that has progressed to Sezary syndrome: a widespread, red, itchy rash (erythroderma) with severe pruritus. Staging finds no visceral involvement. What is the focus of his treatment?
opts: He has no visceral involvement, and splenectomy has no role described for this skin-based lymphoma. Tell: the disease and its treatment are cutaneous.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides and its aggressive form, Sezary syndrome) is focused on the cutaneous manifestations, as there is often no visceral involvement. His erythroderma and pruritus diminish his quality of life.

Rituximab targets CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20) on B cells; his lymphoma is a T-cell disease. Tell: T-cell lymphomas do not usually get the anti-CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20) antibody, and this one is treated at the skin.
The skin lesions resemble fungal infection, but they are lymphoma, not fungus. Tell: the name mycosis fungoides describes the look, not the cause.

set1.q: A 73-year-old man's primary care clinician finds hypercalcemia, anemia and an M-protein, and bone marrow biopsy confirms multiple myeloma. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Orthopedic surgery for the bone lesions
Bone lesions are part of the disease, but myeloma care is led by a hematologist/oncologist, ideally a myeloma expert. Tell: systemic plasma cell cancer goes to hematology/oncology.
His hypercalcemia comes from myeloma activating osteoclasts, not a gland disorder. Tell: treat the cause by referring to hematology/oncology.
Correct. Multiple myeloma requires referral to and management by a hematologist/oncologist, ideally a myeloma expert, with lifelong follow-up for lab monitoring and treatment.
Renal insufficiency is one CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) feature, but the disease itself is managed by a hematologist/oncologist. Tell: refer the cancer, not just one organ it affects.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man has peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified, and is to start a CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone)-type regimen. Which drug used with the B-cell version of this regimen should be left out?
opts: Correct. T-cell lymphomas are treated with similar regimens (CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone)) minus rituximab, because rituximab is an anti-CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20) antibody and T cells do not express CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20).
Cyclophosphamide is part of the regimen for both B-cell and T-cell lymphoma. Tell: the drug removed for T cells is the one aimed at a B-cell surface marker, rituximab.
Doxorubicin stays in the T-cell regimen. Tell: only the antibody that needs CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20) on the cell surface is dropped for T-cell disease.
Prednisone stays in the T-cell regimen. Tell: T cells lack CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20), so rituximab is the one drug left out.

opts: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia usually does not require a bone marrow biopsy for diagnosis; the clone is found in her blood. Tell: the confirming test reads the circulating cells, so the marrow is not sampled first.

Excisional lymph node biopsy diagnoses lymphoma by showing node architecture; she has no lymphadenopathy, and her disease is in the blood. Tell: blood lymphocytosis is confirmed on blood, by flow cytometry.

Serum protein electrophoresis finds the monoclonal protein of plasma cell disorders such as myeloma; it does not identify a clonal B-lymphocyte population. Tell: lymphocytosis calls for flow cytometry, not a protein study.

Correct. Her persistent lymphocytosis above 5,000 suggests chronic lymphocytic leukemia, which is confirmed by flow cytometry identifying a clonal B-cell population (coexpressing CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) and CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5)). It usually does not need a bone marrow biopsy.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia now needs treatment for symptomatic disease. She prefers a time-limited course rather than taking pills indefinitely, even if it is more intensive. Which approach fits her preference?
opts: Observation is for asymptomatic disease without rapid progression; she has symptomatic disease that needs treatment. Tell: once symptoms start, the choice is between continuous and fixed-duration targeted therapy.

Correct. A BCL-2 (B-cell lymphoma 2) inhibitor, venetoclax, is combined with a monoclonal antibody such as obinutuzumab for a fixed duration (infusion plus pill, time limited but more intensive). Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors are usually continuous as monotherapy.

Ibrutinib is a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, usually given continuously as monotherapy, which is the open-ended pill plan she wants to avoid. Tell: the fixed-duration option pairs venetoclax with an antibody.
Acalabrutinib is another Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, also usually continuous when used alone. Tell: her wish for a time-limited course points to venetoclax plus a monoclonal antibody.
set1.cite: 50. Hematologic Malignancies Part II - Gannon.pptx, Slides 11, 13

opts: Bone marrow biopsy is usually not required in chronic lymphocytic leukemia; the diagnosis was made on blood. Tell: the prognostic test is a chromosomal analysis, not a marrow sample.
Advanced imaging is not required to stage chronic lymphocytic leukemia; Rai uses the examination and labs. Tell: prognosis here comes from the chromosomes.
Urine protein electrophoresis looks for the monoclonal light chains of plasma cell disorders such as myeloma. Tell: chronic lymphocytic leukemia prognosis rests on cytogenetics.

Correct. Cytogenetics is important for prognosis and has some treatment considerations. About 80% of cases carry one of four chromosomal abnormalities: deletion 13q, deletion 11q, trisomy 12 or deletion 17p.

opts: Dacarbazine is not the drug being replaced for lung toxicity. Tell: bleomycin is the regimen's pulmonary concern.

Correct. Bleomycin carries pulmonary toxicities, which is why newer agents are replacing it in Hodgkin lymphoma regimens. With pre-existing interstitial lung disease she is the patient in whom bleomycin is most worrying.
Doxorubicin is kept in the regimen; the drug being replaced because of pulmonary toxicity is bleomycin. Tell: her lung disease points to the lung-toxic drug.
Vinblastine is not the drug flagged for pulmonary toxicity. Tell: newer agents are replacing bleomycin, not vinblastine, because of the lungs.

set1.q: A 22-year-old man in the United States has an abdominal mass that has visibly enlarged over 24 hours. Biopsy shows a starry sky pattern (sheets of lymphoma cells with benign macrophages clearing dying cells), consistent with sporadic Burkitt lymphoma. Which referral is appropriate?
opts: A routine visit weeks away ignores a tumor that visibly grows within a day. Tell: Burkitt lymphoma needs emergent referral and rapid transfer of care.
Surgery to remove the mass first
Burkitt lymphoma is treated with multi-agent chemotherapy started promptly; surgery is not the treatment described. Tell: the specialist he needs today is a hematologist.
Repeat imaging and waiting suits indolent disease such as follicular lymphoma; his mass grew over 24 hours. Tell: the fastest lymphoma gets the fastest referral.

Correct. Burkitt lymphoma's doubling time is extremely fast, with tumor expanding within 24 hours, so treatment must start promptly with emergent referral to a hematologist and rapid transfer of care. Early multi-agent chemotherapy gives an excellent prognosis.

set1.q: A 69-year-old man has back pain and constipation. His M-protein is 4.6 g/dL and bone marrow biopsy shows 38% clonal plasma cells. Calcium is 12.1 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5 mg/dL), hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL), creatinine 2.0 mg/dL (normal 0.6-1.2 mg/dL), and imaging shows lytic lesions in the spine. How should his plasma cell disorder be classified?
opts: Correct. Myeloma is diagnosed by at least 10% marrow plasma cells (38%) plus at least one CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) feature; he has all four: hypercalcemia (12.1), renal insufficiency (creatinine 2.0), anemia (9.2) and lytic bone lesions.

His M-protein and plasma cells would fit smoldering myeloma, but smoldering myeloma has no myeloma-defining events, and he has hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions. Tell: CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) features make it myeloma.
That precursor needs an M-protein below 3 g/dL, under 10% plasma cells and no myeloma-defining features; he fails all three. Tell: end-organ damage excludes the asymptomatic precursors.

Reactive hypergammaglobulinemia from cirrhosis or chronic inflammation does not cause clonal marrow plasma cells or lytic lesions. Tell: clonal plasma cells with CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) damage are myeloma.

set1.q: A 71-year-old farmer with years of pesticide exposure has blurred vision and headaches. Serum studies show a large IgM monoclonal protein, and he has signs of hyperviscosity; there are no lytic bone lesions or hypercalcemia. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Smoldering myeloma is an asymptomatic plasma cell disorder; his blurred vision and headaches are hyperviscosity symptoms from an IgM protein. Tell: IgM points to the lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma.
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is defined by lymphocytosis and flow cytometry, and it has no known occupational risk factors. Tell: an IgM protein with hyperviscosity is Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.

Correct. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia) causes excess IgM, a large antibody that causes hyperviscosity with blurred vision and headache. Farming and pesticides are listed risk factors.

Myeloma most commonly makes IgG and presents with CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) features; he has an IgM protein and no lytic lesions or hypercalcemia. Tell: IgM with hyperviscosity is Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.

Five-fold is half the figure; same-sex siblings carry a 10-fold increased risk. Tell: same sex, ten times.

Correct. Same-sex siblings of a patient with Hodgkin lymphoma have a 10-fold increased risk of also developing it. Epstein-Barr virus is a suspected risk factor (found in 40-50% of cases), with HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), human herpesvirus 6 and tuberculosis also listed.

set1.q: A 46-year-old man has a 3-cm firm, painless left axillary lymph node that has grown over 6 weeks. There is no infection to explain it. Which test establishes the diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Lymphoma is diagnosed by excisional lymph node biopsy, reserved for significant enlargement (2 cm), persistent and progressively enlarging nodes; his 3-cm growing node qualifies. Excision shows the node architecture needed for the diagnosis.
Fine-needle aspiration should be avoided: excisional biopsy is required to see lymph node architecture, and aspiration may miss the diagnosis. Tell: the whole node is needed.
Flow cytometry of blood confirms chronic lymphocytic leukemia, a disease of blood lymphocytosis; his problem is an enlarging node. Tell: a suspicious node is excised.

set1.q: A 68-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia confirmed by flow cytometry has an absolute lymphocyte count of 22,000 per microliter (normal 1,000-4,000). She has painless, firm, mobile cervical and axillary lymph nodes; the liver and spleen are not enlarged. Hemoglobin is 13.1 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL) and platelets 210,000 per microliter (normal 150,000-450,000). What is her Rai stage?
opts: Stage 0 is asymptomatic lymphocytosis with no other finding, but she has palpable cervical and axillary nodes. Tell: adding lymphadenopathy to lymphocytosis moves the stage up to I.

Correct. Item by item: lymphocytosis yes (22,000); lymphadenopathy yes (cervical and axillary nodes); organomegaly no; anemia no (13.1 g/dL); thrombocytopenia no (210,000). Lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy and nothing more is Rai stage I.
Stage II adds organomegaly (hepatomegaly and/or splenomegaly) to lymphocytosis and lymphadenopathy; her liver and spleen are not enlarged. Tell: nodes without an organ finding stop at stage I.
Stage III needs anemia with the lymphocytosis; her hemoglobin of 13.1 g/dL sits inside 12.0-15.5 g/dL. Tell: Rai stages III and IV are driven by low blood counts, and hers are normal.

set1.q: A 76-year-old man has had chronic lymphocytic leukemia, observed without treatment, for 6 years. Over 3 weeks one cervical lymph node has grown rapidly, and he now has fevers, night sweats and weight loss. Which complication has most likely occurred?
opts: Monoclonal B lymphocytosis is the precursor that progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia at 1-2% per year, not a complication of it. Tell: the move here is from leukemia to an aggressive lymphoma.

Smoldering myeloma is an intermediate-stage clonal plasma cell disorder, not a complication of chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and it does not explain a rapidly growing node. Tell: a fast-growing node with B symptoms in this leukemia is Richter transformation.

Correct. Richter transformation is chronic lymphocytic leukemia transforming into an aggressive B-cell lymphoma, with poor outcomes. A long, stable course that suddenly turns into a rapidly growing node with B symptoms is that picture.

Tumor lysis syndrome is a medical emergency of rapid tumor breakdown that releases potassium, phosphorus and uric acid; it is a chemical crisis, not one node growing over weeks. Tell: a growing node with B symptoms is transformation, not lysis.

set1.q: A 62-year-old woman's excisional lymph node biopsy shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Which study is required next to characterize and stage her disease?
opts: Physical examination and blood counts alone for staging
Staging from the examination and labs alone is the Rai approach for chronic lymphocytic leukemia, which needs no advanced imaging. Tell: lymphoma staging requires imaging of the node regions.
Fine-needle aspiration of each remaining node
Fine-needle aspiration is avoided in lymphoma because it cannot show node architecture; staging is done by imaging. Tell: map the disease with computed tomography or positron emission tomography.
Serum protein electrophoresis for monoclonal protein

A monoclonal protein on serum protein electrophoresis is characteristic of multiple myeloma; it does not stage lymphoma. Tell: lymphoma staging is about where the nodes and organs are, which imaging shows.
Computed tomography or positron emission tomography

Correct. Imaging, usually computed tomography or positron emission tomography, is required to characterize and appropriately stage lymphoma by the Lugano classification. Work-up also includes a complete blood count, chemistries, lactate dehydrogenase and bone marrow biopsy.

set1.q: A 67-year-old man has diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with involved lymph nodes in the neck and the groin and no extranodal sites. His ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) performance status is 1, and his lactate dehydrogenase is above the upper limit of normal. How many poor-prognosis factors does he have?
opts: One factor would count only his age (67); his nodes above and below the diaphragm make stage III, and his lactate dehydrogenase is elevated. Tell: count the stage and the lab as well.
Two misses one item: age over 60, stage III (nodes on both sides of the diaphragm) and elevated lactate dehydrogenase each count. Tell: the commonly missed one is stage, read from the node map.

Correct. Item by item from the poor-prognosis list: age over 60, yes (67); extranodal sites, no; ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) status above 2, no (1); stage III or IV, yes (neck and groin nodes span the diaphragm, stage III); elevated lactate dehydrogenase, yes. Total 3.
Four double-counts: his ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) status of 1 is not above 2, and he has no extranodal sites. Tell: only age, stage III and lactate dehydrogenase count.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman has diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Staging shows enlarged cervical lymph nodes, lymphoma deposits in the liver, and bone marrow biopsy involvement. What is her stage?
opts: Stage 1 is a single node region or a single organ; she has nodes plus two organs. Tell: more than one organ is never localized disease.
Stage 2 is two or more node regions on one side of the diaphragm, without organ spread; she has liver and marrow disease. Tell: organ spread outranks the node count.
Stage 3 is nodes above and below the diaphragm; her defining finding is disease in multiple organs. Tell: liver plus marrow is widespread, stage 4.
Correct. Lymphoma in the liver and the bone marrow is widespread disease with multiple organs involved, which is stage 4 with or without lymph node involvement. Her cervical nodes do not change that.

opts: Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia requires referral to, and management by, a hematologist/oncologist, even when asymptomatic and observed. Treatment choice depends on patient preferences and mutations, and follow-up includes lab monitoring.
Infections are a complication of ineffective white cells, but the leukemia itself is managed by a hematologist/oncologist. Tell: a confirmed clonal leukemia goes to hematology/oncology.
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is not treated surgically, and she has no node to remove. Tell: diagnosis was made on blood and care is with hematology/oncology.
Asymptomatic disease may be observed, but the deck states the disease requires referral to and management by a hematologist/oncologist. Tell: watch and wait is still done by the specialist.

set2.q: A 63-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging neck mass with fevers, night sweats and weight loss. Excisional biopsy shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and staging shows nodes above and below the diaphragm. Which regimen is typical?
opts: Rituximab with cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone

Correct. Aggressive B-cell lymphomas such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma are often treated with multi-drug chemotherapy, for example R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone). Rituximab targets the CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20) on B cells.
Cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone without rituximab

Dropping rituximab is the T-cell lymphoma approach, because T cells lack CD20 (cluster of differentiation 20). Her lymphoma is B-cell, so rituximab is kept. Tell: B-cell disease gets the R in the regimen.
Doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine and dacarbazine for two cycles

Doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine and dacarbazine is a Hodgkin lymphoma regimen, not diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Tell: an aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma gets rituximab-based multi-drug chemotherapy.
Radiation to the largest involved node region as the single therapy
Radiation alone is for single-node, non-aggressive disease; hers is aggressive and spans the diaphragm. Tell: aggressive, widespread B-cell lymphoma needs multi-drug chemotherapy.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man has painless, firm, mobile lymph nodes in the neck and both axillae. His absolute lymphocyte count is 4,500 per microliter (normal 1,000-4,000), and flow cytometry shows a clonal B-cell population coexpressing CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) and CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5). How should this be classified?
opts: Atypical lymphocytosis with infections such as pertussis is reactive, while his flow cytometry shows a clonal B-cell population. Tell: a clone with the CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) and CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5) pattern is leukemia, not infection.
ruled out by a stated finding

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma is diagnosed by excisional node biopsy and expresses CD15 (cluster of differentiation 15) and CD30 (cluster of differentiation 30), not a circulating CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5) clone. Tell: the blood clone points to chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is diagnosed with a count above 5,000 for 3 months or a count below 5,000 with lymphadenopathy or other symptoms. His count is 4,500, but he has lymphadenopathy, and the clone coexpresses CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) and CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5).

Monoclonal B lymphocytosis is a count below 5,000 with no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms; his neck and axillary nodes exclude it. Tell: a sub-5,000 count plus lymphadenopathy is chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 57-year-old man has a non-aggressive (low-grade) B-cell lymphoma confined to a single lymph node region in the left groin; staging shows no other disease. Which treatment fits this presentation?
opts: Ibrutinib is a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: a single-node, non-aggressive lymphoma is radiated.
Allogeneic stem cell transplant is not the treatment for a single node of non-aggressive disease; that presentation is radiated. Tell: one node, low grade, radiation.
Correct. Management depends on subtype and presentation: a single node of non-aggressive disease is treated with radiation. His staging shows one region only (stage 1) of low-grade disease.
Multi-drug chemotherapy is for aggressive B-cell lymphomas; his disease is low-grade and in one node region. Tell: single node and non-aggressive points to radiation.

set2.q: A 24-year-old man has newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma, a high-grade lymphoma. Excisional biopsy, imaging, blood counts, chemistries and lactate dehydrogenase have been done. Which additional procedure is required in his work-up?
opts: Protein electrophoresis looks for the monoclonal protein of plasma cell disorders. Tell: Burkitt lymphoma's added work-up step is a lumbar puncture.

Correct. High-grade lymphomas, including Burkitt lymphoma, require a lumbar puncture as part of the work-up, alongside bone marrow biopsy, imaging, a complete blood count, chemistries and lactate dehydrogenase.
Fine-needle aspiration is avoided in lymphoma work-up, and his diagnosis is already made by excisional biopsy. Tell: the extra step for a high-grade lymphoma is a lumbar puncture.

opts: Stage 1 is a single lymph node region or a single organ; he has two separate node regions. Tell: a second region on the same side moves the stage to 2.

He spends most of the day in a chair, with an ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) performance status of 3, and his lactate dehydrogenase is elevated. How many poor-prognosis factors does he have?
opts: One counts only his age; his performance status of 3, stage III node map and elevated lactate dehydrogenase all count too. Tell: work through all five items.
Two misses two items; age, a performance status above 2, stage III and elevated lactate dehydrogenase all apply. Tell: nodes on both sides of the diaphragm are stage III.
Three misses one item, usually the stage; axillary plus inguinal nodes span the diaphragm (stage III). Tell: his only absent factor is extranodal disease.

Correct. Item by item: age over 60, yes (72); extranodal sites, no; ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) status above 2, yes (3); stage III or IV, yes (axillary nodes above and inguinal nodes below the diaphragm, stage III); elevated lactate dehydrogenase, yes. Total 4.

set2.q: A 72-year-old woman has newly diagnosed multiple myeloma. Her beta-2 microglobulin is 6.8 mg/L (normal 0.8-2.2 mg/L), albumin 3.9 g/dL (normal 3.5-5.0 g/dL), chromosomal studies show deletion 17p, and lactate dehydrogenase is above the upper limit of normal. What is her R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) stage?
opts: Stage I needs beta-2 microglobulin below 3.5 mg/L, standard-risk chromosomes and normal lactate dehydrogenase; she fails all three. Tell: a normal albumin alone cannot make stage I.
Stage II is anyone who is neither stage I nor III; she meets every stage III item. Tell: high beta-2 microglobulin, deletion 17p and high lactate dehydrogenase together are stage III.

Correct. R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) stage III: beta-2 microglobulin at least 5.5 mg/L regardless of albumin (6.8), high-risk chromosomal abnormalities (deletion 17p), and high lactate dehydrogenase. She meets all three, so her normal albumin does not matter.
The R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) table stops at stage III. Tell: her high-risk findings put her in the highest stage, III.

set2.q: A 75-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia has been observed for 2 years. She has no symptoms, but her absolute lymphocyte count has risen from 18,000 to 41,000 per microliter (normal 1,000-4,000) over 4 months. What is the next step?
opts: Watch and wait suits asymptomatic disease without rapid progression; her count more than doubled in 4 months. Tell: a doubling time under 6 months ends observation even without symptoms.
Repeat the count in a year
Waiting a year ignores a lymphocyte count that more than doubled in 4 months, which is the definition of rapid progression. Tell: doubling in under 6 months is an indication to treat.
A bone marrow biopsy is usually not required to diagnose chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and rapid progression is itself the indication for treatment. Tell: the count doubling in 4 months decides.

Correct. Observation lasts until rapid progression or disease-related symptoms. Her count has more than doubled in 4 months, under the 6-month mark, which is rapid progression and an indication to treat, with targeted therapies such as a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

set2.q: A 67-year-old woman has classical Hodgkin lymphoma of the mixed cellularity subtype, stage II and not bulky. Which features of her case predict inferior results?
opts: Neither sex nor stage II spread is listed among the factors predicting inferior Hodgkin results; those are older age, bulky disease and the lymphocyte-depleted or mixed cellularity subtypes. Tell: look at her age and subtype.

Her mixed cellularity subtype counts, but stage II is early disease, treated with chemotherapy, and is not named as a predictor of inferior results. Tell: her age, not her stage, is the second named factor.
Older age counts, and bulky disease does predict inferior results, but her disease is stated not to be bulky. Tell: her risk factors are age and the mixed cellularity subtype.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 72-year-old Black man has 2 months of back and pelvic pain, constipation, increased thirst, urinary frequency, fatigue and ankle swelling. Calcium is 11.9 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5 mg/dL), hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL) and creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (normal 0.6-1.2 mg/dL); skull x-ray shows multiple punched-out lytic lesions. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. His findings are the CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) features: hypercalcemia (constipation, thirst, urinary frequency), renal insufficiency (swelling), anemia (fatigue) and bone pain with punched-out osteolytic lesions. Age over 65 and African American race raise myeloma risk.
Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia makes IgM and causes hyperviscosity (blurred vision, headache), not hypercalcemia and lytic bone lesions. Tell: punched-out lesions with high calcium are myeloma.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia shows lymphocytosis and painless lymphadenopathy, not hypercalcemia or lytic skull lesions. Tell: the CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) pattern points to a plasma cell malignancy.
Hodgkin lymphoma presents with painless cervical nodes, a mediastinal mass and pruritus, not lytic bone lesions with renal failure. Tell: calcium, kidneys, anemia and bones together are myeloma.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man has chronic lymphocytic leukemia, Rai stage 0, found on routine blood work. He has no symptoms, and his absolute lymphocyte count of 12,000 per microliter (normal 1,000-4,000) has been stable for 9 months. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: He has no lymphadenopathy, and excision is a lymphoma diagnostic biopsy, not a treatment for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: asymptomatic stable disease is simply observed.

Correct. Asymptomatic patients may be observed (watch and wait) until there is rapid progression (lymphocyte count doubling in under 6 months) or disease-related symptoms. Treatment begins with symptomatic disease or rapid progression; he has neither.

Ibrutinib, a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is a targeted therapy for disease that needs treatment, which begins with symptoms or rapid progression. His count is stable and he has no symptoms. Tell: no symptoms and no doubling means watch and wait.

Venetoclax with a monoclonal antibody is a fixed-duration targeted regimen for disease that needs treatment; asymptomatic, stable disease does not. Tell: therapy starts at symptoms or a doubling under 6 months.

set2.q: A 19-year-old man with sporadic Burkitt lymphoma is about to begin multi-agent chemotherapy. His potassium, phosphorus, uric acid and creatinine are currently normal. What should be done before the first dose?
opts: Burkitt lymphoma treatment must start promptly; its doubling time is extremely fast. Tell: prevent tumor lysis with allopurinol and fluids, then treat without delay.

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome should be anticipated in aggressive lymphoma, and Burkitt lymphoma needs caution when therapy starts. Patients are given allopurinol (a hypouricemic agent) and fluids in advance, with aggressive intravenous hydration.
Restrict fluids to protect the kidneys

Fluid restriction is the reverse of what is needed; tumor lysis is prevented with aggressive intravenous hydration plus allopurinol. Tell: fluids protect the tubules from uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals.
Tumor breakdown releases potassium, and hyperkalemia with arrhythmia is the largest risk of tumor lysis. Tell: adding potassium before lysis is the wrong direction.

set2.q: A 77-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia confirmed by flow cytometry reports fatigue. Her absolute lymphocyte count is 56,000 per microliter (normal 1,000-4,000). She has axillary lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL) and platelets 182,000 per microliter (normal 150,000-450,000). What is her Rai stage?
opts: Stage I is lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy alone; she also has splenomegaly and a hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL. Tell: once anemia is present, the nodes no longer decide the stage.

Stage II fits her nodes and spleen, but her hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL adds anemia, which defines stage III with or without nodes and organomegaly. Tell: a low hemoglobin outranks organ findings in Rai staging.

Correct. Item by item: lymphocytosis yes (56,000); lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly yes; anemia yes (9.4 g/dL, below 12.0); thrombocytopenia no (182,000). Lymphocytosis with anemia is stage III, with or without nodes and organomegaly, so the anemia sets the stage.
Stage IV is lymphocytosis with thrombocytopenia; her platelets are 182,000 per microliter, inside the normal range. Tell: anemia without a low platelet count stops at stage III.

set2.q: A 28-year-old man with Burkitt lymphoma started multi-agent chemotherapy 36 hours ago. His potassium is 6.6 mEq/L (normal 3.5-5.0 mEq/L), phosphorus 7.8 mg/dL (normal 2.5-4.5 mg/dL), uric acid 13.1 mg/dL (normal 3.5-7.2 mg/dL) and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (normal 0.6-1.2 mg/dL). Which complication has developed?
opts: Richter transformation is chronic lymphocytic leukemia turning into an aggressive B-cell lymphoma, not a lab emergency after chemotherapy. Tell: high potassium, phosphorus and uric acid after treatment are tumor lysis.

Myeloma activates osteoclasts and raises calcium; his labs show high potassium, phosphorus and uric acid after chemotherapy for Burkitt lymphoma. Tell: cell contents released all at once mean tumor lysis.

Hyperviscosity comes from excess IgM in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, causing blurred vision and headache; it does not raise potassium or uric acid. Tell: this pattern after chemotherapy is tumor lysis syndrome.

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome is rapid tumor breakdown releasing potassium, phosphorus and uric acid; uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals in the renal tubules cause acute renal failure. It is a medical emergency, expected after treatment of aggressive lymphoma such as Burkitt.

set2.q: A 64-year-old woman has newly diagnosed symptomatic multiple myeloma. Which initial regimen is used?
opts: Venetoclax with obinutuzumab for a fixed duration
Venetoclax with a monoclonal antibody for a fixed duration is a chronic lymphocytic leukemia option. Tell: myeloma's 3- or 4-drug regimen is built on a proteasome inhibitor and immunomodulatory drug.
Proteasome inhibitor, immunomodulatory drug and steroid

Correct. Newly diagnosed patients are treated with a 3- or 4-drug regimen with a proteasome inhibitor and immunomodulatory drug backbone with steroids. The goal is prolonged remission to improve survival and quality of life, as myeloma is incurable.
Rituximab-based multi-drug chemotherapy is used for aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: myeloma's backbone is a proteasome inhibitor plus an immunomodulatory drug with steroids.
That four-drug regimen is the historical Hodgkin lymphoma treatment. Tell: newly diagnosed myeloma gets a proteasome inhibitor, an immunomodulatory drug and steroids.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. set2.q: A 66-year-old man has newly diagnosed multiple myeloma. His beta-2 microglobulin is 2.9 mg/L (normal 0.8-2.2 mg/L), albumin 4.0 g/dL (normal 3.5-5.0 g/dL), chromosomal studies show only standard-risk abnormalities, and lactate dehydrogenase is normal. What is his R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) stage?
opts: Correct. R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) stage I requires every item: beta-2 microglobulin below 3.5 mg/L (2.9), albumin at least 3.5 g/dL (4.0), standard-risk chromosomal abnormalities, and normal lactate dehydrogenase. He meets all four. The stage is prognostic and does not broadly change treatment.
Stage II is any patient who is not stage I or III; he meets every stage I item. Tell: below 3.5 mg/L, albumin 3.5 or more, standard risk and normal lactate dehydrogenase is stage I.

Stage III needs beta-2 microglobulin of at least 5.5 mg/L with high-risk chromosomes (deletion 17p, t(4;14) or t(14;16)) and high lactate dehydrogenase; he has none of these. Tell: all four of his values are favorable.
The R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) table has three stages; there is no stage IV. Tell: his favorable values put him in stage I, the lowest.

set2.q: A 68-year-old woman with splenomegaly is found to have splenic marginal zone lymphoma. Which associated infection should be tested for?
opts: Correct. Splenic marginal zone lymphoma is associated with hepatitis C; marginal zone lymphomas are more common in older adults. Her splenic subtype points to hepatitis C rather than Helicobacter pylori.
Helicobacter pylori is associated with gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (about two-thirds of cases), not the splenic subtype. Tell: the organ decides, and hers is the spleen.
Epstein-Barr virus is strongly associated with endemic Burkitt lymphoma. Tell: the infection linked to splenic marginal zone lymphoma is hepatitis C.

Lyme disease is listed among chronic infections raising non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk in general, but the named link for the splenic marginal zone subtype is hepatitis C. Tell: spleen pairs with hepatitis C.

set2.q: A 63-year-old woman has an M-protein of 3.9 g/dL, and bone marrow biopsy shows 24% clonal plasma cells. She has no symptoms; calcium, creatinine and hemoglobin are normal, and whole-body imaging shows no bone lesions. How should her plasma cell disorder be classified?
opts: Correct. Reading the criteria: M-protein above 3 g/dL (3.9) and marrow plasma cells within 10-60% (24%), with no myeloma-defining events (no anemia, bone lesions, renal failure or hypercalcemia). That is smoldering myeloma, an intermediate stage that typically does not require treatment.
That precursor needs an M-protein below 3 g/dL and fewer than 10% plasma cells; she has 3.9 g/dL and 24%. Tell: both values cross the thresholds into the intermediate stage.

Myeloma needs at least one CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone) feature with the marrow plasma cells; her calcium, kidneys, hemoglobin and bones are normal. Tell: high numbers without end-organ damage is smoldering.
Reactive hypergammaglobulinemia follows cirrhosis or chronic inflammation, and she has 24% clonal plasma cells. Tell: a clonal marrow population with a large M-protein is a plasma cell disorder.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman has excisional biopsy-proven diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Computed tomography and positron emission tomography show disease confined to one group of right cervical lymph nodes, with no other nodes or organs involved. What is her stage?
opts: Correct. Lugano staging, a modified Ann Arbor system: stage 1 is localized disease in a single lymph node region or a single organ. One right cervical node region with nothing else involved is stage 1.
Stage 2 needs two or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm; she has one node region. Tell: count the node regions first, and hers is one.
Stage 3 needs node regions both above and below the diaphragm; her single region is in the neck only. Tell: nothing below the diaphragm means stage 3 is impossible.
Stage 4 is widespread disease in multiple organs, with or without nodes; she has no organ involvement. Tell: one node region is localized, the lowest stage.

set2.q: A 78-year-old woman has just been told she has chronic lymphocytic leukemia, Rai stage 0. She asks what her long-term outlook is. Which statement is accurate?
opts: It is cured by a short chemotherapy course

Treatment is targeted therapy, continuous pills or a time-limited infusion plus pill, and it is not described as a short curative course; asymptomatic disease is simply observed. Tell: the outlook is long survival with the disease, not cure.
It turns into aggressive lymphoma in a year
Richter transformation to an aggressive B-cell lymphoma is a risk with poor outcomes, but it is not the expected course. Tell: most patients live long with this leukemia.
She is likely to die with it, not of it

Correct. Five-year relative survival is about 88%, much improved by novel agents, and the elderly age at onset with ongoing new therapies means many patients will die with chronic lymphocytic leukemia rather than from it. Long-term prognosis is likely very good.
She is likely to die of it in 2 years
Survival is far better: about 88% are alive at 5 years in the modern era. Tell: in an elderly patient this leukemia is usually something she lives with.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man has classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Staging imaging shows involved left cervical lymph nodes and right inguinal lymph nodes, with no liver, bone marrow or other organ involvement. What is his stage?
opts: Stage 1 is a single node region or single organ; he has two regions. Tell: more than one region is never stage 1.
Stage 2 keeps every region on one side of the diaphragm; his neck and groin are on opposite sides. Tell: crossing the diaphragm is stage 3.

Correct. Cervical nodes are above the diaphragm and inguinal nodes below it; with no organ involvement, two or more node regions above and below the diaphragm is stage 3. His age over 60 is the second peak of Hodgkin lymphoma's bimodal incidence.
Stage 4 needs widespread organ involvement, and he has none. Tell: nodes on both sides without organs stop at stage 3.

set2.q: A 59-year-old man with chronic dyspepsia has an endoscopic gastric biopsy showing extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Which associated infection should be tested for?
opts: Correct. Gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, the most common extranodal marginal zone subtype, is associated with Helicobacter pylori in about two-thirds of cases. A stomach lymphoma of this type calls for testing for it.
Hepatitis C is associated with the splenic marginal zone subtype, not the gastric mucosa-associated type. Tell: stomach goes with Helicobacter pylori, spleen with hepatitis C.

Epstein-Barr virus is strongly associated with endemic Burkitt lymphoma and is suspected in Hodgkin lymphoma, not gastric marginal zone lymphoma. Tell: gastric lymphoma of mucosal tissue links to Helicobacter pylori.
Human T-lymphotropic virus 1 is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, a very aggressive T-cell disease. Tell: his lymphoma is a B-cell marginal zone type of the stomach.

set2.q: A 30-year-old woman with aggressive lymphoma develops tumor lysis syndrome on day 2 of chemotherapy, with rising potassium, phosphorus, uric acid and creatinine. Which consequence of this syndrome carries the largest risk?
opts: Acute renal failure from uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals in the tubules does occur and exacerbates the syndrome, but the largest risk named is hyperkalemia with arrhythmia. Tell: the greatest danger is the heart rhythm.
Constipation, thirst and urinary frequency come from the hypercalcemia of multiple myeloma, not tumor lysis. Tell: tumor lysis releases potassium, and the danger is arrhythmia.
Stroke from hyperviscosity is a rare result of excess IgM in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. Tell: in tumor lysis syndrome, high potassium causing arrhythmia is the largest risk.

Correct. The largest risk of tumor lysis syndrome is hyperkalemia leading to arrhythmia and potential death. Acute renal failure from uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals also occurs and worsens the condition, but the potassium is the killer.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman has an absolute lymphocyte count of 4,600 per microliter (normal 1,000-4,000) on routine blood work. Flow cytometry shows a clonal B-cell population. She has no symptoms, no lymphadenopathy and no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly; hemoglobin and platelets are normal. How should this finding be classified?
opts: Correct. Her absolute lymphocyte count is elevated but below 5,000 per microliter, and she has no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms. That is monoclonal B lymphocytosis, which progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia at about 1-2% per year.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia needs a count above 5,000 per microliter for 3 months, or a count below 5,000 with lymphadenopathy or other symptoms; she has 4,600 and no nodes or symptoms. Tell: a sub-5,000 count with a clean examination is monoclonal B lymphocytosis.
Atypical lymphocytosis from infections such as pertussis is reactive, not a clonal B-cell population, and she has no infection. Tell: flow cytometry showing a clone points away from a reactive cause.
ruled out by a stated finding

Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma producing excess IgM with hyperviscosity (blurred vision, headache); she has none of this. Tell: a small clonal B-cell count with no other findings is monoclonal B lymphocytosis.

set2.q: A 24-year-old woman has a painless, rubbery left cervical lymph node that aches after she drinks alcohol, and intense itching for 2 months. Chest x-ray shows a mediastinal mass. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Her features (node pain with alcohol, intense pruritus, a mediastinal mass on chest x-ray, age in her 20s) are listed for Hodgkin lymphoma, not Burkitt lymphoma. Tell: alcohol pain and itching point to Hodgkin lymphoma.
Follicular lymphoma does not explain node pain with alcohol, intense pruritus and a mediastinal mass, the Hodgkin lymphoma features she shows. Tell: those three features are classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal incidence with a peak in adults in their 20s and presents with painless lymphadenopathy, usually cervical, that may hurt with alcohol, intense pruritus and a mediastinal mass on chest x-ray. Her picture matches item by item.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia does not fit: node pain with alcohol, intense pruritus and a mediastinal mass in a woman in her 20s are Hodgkin lymphoma features. Tell: a 24-year-old with node pain after alcohol and a mediastinal mass is Hodgkin lymphoma.

set2.q: A 29-year-old man has classical Hodgkin lymphoma with cervical nodes and a bulky mediastinal mass, all above the diaphragm, and drenching night sweats. Which treatment approach is appropriate?
opts: Radiation alone is the plan for a single node of non-aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, not for Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: bulky Hodgkin lymphoma with B symptoms needs chemotherapy plus radiation.
Watch and wait fits indolent follicular lymphoma, not bulky Hodgkin lymphoma with night sweats. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma is generally curable and is treated.

Correct. His nodes are on one side of the diaphragm (stage II), and the disease is bulky with B symptoms (night sweats). Bulky stage I or II disease, or disease with B symptoms, is treated with chemotherapy plus radiation.
A short course of chemotherapy is for early stage I or II disease that is not bulky and has no B symptoms; he has a bulky mass and night sweats. Tell: bulky or B symptoms add radiation.

set2.q: A 58-year-old man with multiple myeloma has responded to initial 3-drug therapy and is a transplant candidate. Which plan has been shown to improve overall survival?
opts: Watch and wait suits smoldering myeloma or indolent lymphoma, not active myeloma in a transplant candidate. Tell: transplant then maintenance improves survival.

Correct. For a transplant candidate, autologous transplant has been shown to improve overall survival, as has maintenance therapy after transplant. Most patients still relapse and need continuous therapy for disease control.
Myeloma is incurable and most patients relapse; maintenance after transplant improves survival, and continuous therapy keeps control. Tell: remission is maintained, not left alone.
Radiation alone is the plan for a single-node, non-aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, not systemic myeloma. Tell: a fit myeloma patient goes to autologous transplant.

set2.q: A 9-year-old boy from sub-Saharan Africa has a painless jaw swelling that his mother says grew visibly over a single day. He has fever, night sweats and weight loss, and the tumor cells test positive for Epstein-Barr virus. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hodgkin lymphoma spreads to contiguous nodes in an orderly fashion, usually as a painless cervical node in adults in their 20s or over 60; it does not grow visibly within a day. Tell: overnight growth in an African child with Epstein-Barr virus is Burkitt.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults and can grow fast, but the endemic African, Epstein-Barr virus-linked jaw tumor of a child is Burkitt. Tell: a child, Africa and same-day growth.
Follicular lymphoma is indolent, with waxing and waning painless nodes over months to years. Tell: visible growth within a day is the opposite of indolent.

Correct. Burkitt lymphoma is a very aggressive lymphoma with very rapidly growing, often painless swelling (changes visible within a day) and B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss). The endemic type is seen in sub-Saharan Africa and strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus.

set2.q: A 34-year-old woman being treated for laboratory-confirmed pertussis has an absolute lymphocyte count of 7,900 per microliter (normal 1,000-4,000) with atypical lymphocytes on the smear. She has no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. What is the best interpretation of her lymphocytosis?
opts: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia needs a clonal B-cell population on flow cytometry, usually in an older adult (median age 70), and a count above 5,000 persisting 3 months. Tell: her count rose during a proven pertussis infection.
Monoclonal B lymphocytosis is a clonal count below 5,000; hers is 7,900 and explained by pertussis. Tell: an infection-linked atypical lymphocytosis is reactive, not a monoclonal disorder.
ruled out by a stated finding
Burkitt lymphoma presents with a very rapidly growing, often painless swelling and B symptoms; she has no mass. Tell: atypical lymphocytes during a known infection are reactive.

Correct. Atypical lymphocytosis can be seen with some infections, including pertussis, which is on the differential of chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Her proven infection, young age (that leukemia has a median age of 70) and clean examination fit a reactive cause.
